title: Using translations
hook: a pun dies in the subtitles; the Granth's first character is a digit no English can carry
tomorrow: so if the English helps, why read the Gurmukhi at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, santhiaa: a teacher and a student, one line, again and again, until the sound settles. A teacher's ear. But a lot of people meet the Granth first through somebody else's ear: a translator's.
screen: `SANTHIAA: A TEACHER'S EAR.` → `AND A TRANSLATOR'S EAR?`

segments.voice: A movie character makes a pun, the subtitles translate it, and nobody in the theater laughs. The joke didn't survive the trip. Here's a stranger case. The very first character in the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter. It's a digit: the number one, written in Gurmukhi, joined to the sign for Onkar. Ik Onkar. Every English translation has to turn that digit into words. So, the puzzle: can an English line hand you what's on the page?
screen: `THE PUN DIED IN THE SUBTITLES.` → `THE FIRST CHARACTER: A DIGIT.` → `CAN ENGLISH CARRY IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the help. In 1909, Max Arthur Macauliffe published The Sikh Religion, with English renderings of the Gurus' hymns, and later translators made their own. For anyone who can't yet read Gurmukhi, they open a door. This path leans on them too, mostly in paraphrase. Now the puzzle. Macauliffe's English of the Mul Mantar opens with words about there being one God. Another version says one creator. Another just says the One. None of them is wrong, and none of them is a digit. The page says one the way a number says it: plain, before any description. Each translator has to choose, and every choice keeps something and drops something. It happens again two words later. Sat naam: one English reads it as whose name is true, another as truth is the name. Same Gurmukhi, two shades. So here's the answer. Yes, translations help, a lot. And each is partial, a window on one side of the house. Read two side by side and the differences show you where the Gurmukhi holds more than either. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture begins with a number, and no English sentence can quite be a number.
screen: `1909: MACAULIFFE'S ENGLISH.` · `ONE GOD? ONE CREATOR? THE ONE?` · `SAT NAAM: TWO SHADES.` · `READ TWO SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `TRANSLATIONS HELP.`

segments.voice: Find the Mul Mantar's opening in two English versions, in an app, a book or online. Look at them side by side and find one word where they differ. Then let your eyes rest on the Gurmukhi above them, on the digit one, and breathe slowly, letting it be one before it's any word.
Using translations: reading the Granth with English renderings, like Macauliffe's of 1909 and later ones, as real help that is always partial. The eleventh word of the year.
For the road: translations help, and two of them side by side help more than one. Eleven of twenty.

notes: v3 puzzle day: the Granth's first character is a numeral (੧ in ੴ); every English version must turn it into words and choose (one God, one creator, the One). Answer: translations help and each is partial.

Macauliffe's rendering is paraphrased ('opens with words about there being one God'), not quoted, because the exact 1909 wording wasn't verified. The year 1909 and the title The Sikh Religion come from the outline and the work itself. Confirm.
'Another version says one creator. Another just says the One' describes renderings in general use without naming any modern (copyrighted) translator. Confirm fair.
Sat naam: 'whose name is true' and 'truth is the name' as two common readings. Confirm.
